title: Korea’s alphabet was designed so its letters picture the mouth
body: In the 1440s, King Sejong the Great introduced a new script because Chinese characters fit the Korean language poorly and took years to master, leaving most people unable to read. Announced around 1443–44 and published in 1446, Hangul arranges its letters into syllable blocks. Its consonant shapes were explained as diagrams of the speech organs, an unusually deliberate design for a writing system.

slides.heading: Letters as anatomy
slides.text: ㄱ (k) sketches the back of the tongue raised, ㄴ (n) the tongue touching the roof of the mouth, ㅁ (m) the mouth, ㅅ (s) a tooth and ㅇ the throat.

slides.heading: Add a stroke
slides.text: Related sounds share a shape. An extra stroke marks a harsher, aspirated sound: ㄱ (k) becomes ㅋ (kh), and ㄷ (t) becomes ㅌ (th).

slides.heading: Three building blocks
slides.text: Vowels grow from a dot, a flat line and an upright line, which the original text tied to cosmic ideas. ㅏ, for example, is ㅣ plus the dot.

slides.heading: How a Hangul syllable is built

steps.label: ㄱ sketches the back of the tongue raised
Add a stroke for a harsher sound: ㄱ to ㅋ
Vowels: a dot, a flat line, an upright line
Stack the letters into one syllable block

slides.heading: A slow victory
slides.text: Elites who prized Chinese learning looked down on Hangul for centuries, and a king persecuted its use in 1504. It became the government’s preferred script only in 1894.

slides.question: What does an extra stroke on a Hangul consonant mark?
slides.explanation: Related sounds share a shape, and an extra stroke marks aspiration: ㄱ (k) becomes ㅋ (kh), and ㄷ (t) becomes ㅌ (th).
